title: ‘Suro’ Director Mikel Gurrea on ‘Saints,’ Directing ‘The Belovd’ Star Victoria Luengo,  Religious-Art Theft and Finding Mystery in Care

body:
For director Mikel Gurrea’s latest he didn’t have to travel far in search of a story.

	“I live in Barcelona’s district of Sants and, having done my previous film in the woods, this time I wanted to find fiction at my doorstep,” Gurrea told Variety of “Saints,” picked up for international by M-Appeal.

	“So I started interrogating that name, Sants, which means Saints in Catalan.”


	His curiosity led him to a church, a locked one.
	

	“Every time I passed by, I found it closed. So I thought, a closed church is almost like a vault. Someone could steal it and I started reading about religious art robberies.”

	But before the mechanics of the thefts could take over, the character of Lali arrived.

	“The very first thing I wrote was Lali crying in a hospital chapel looking at the statue of a saint, at night. Once the other person in the chapel left, Lali dried her tears instantly, like an actress who was playing a role to get her way, she got up and stole the statue.”

	Immediately, she was difficult to pin down: a thief who might also be grieving, a performer whose performance like the best of them still contains something real.

	“There was an ambivalence there, a playfulness and perhaps some real sorrow too. I started following this character and everything else came from that scene.”

	That ambivalence extends to Lali’s relationship with her estranged mother, Gloria played by Ariadna Gil (“Pans Labyrinth”). A woman whose instinct is to disappear finds herself wrenched back to Barcelona and into a role that demands precisely the opposite: staying put and caring for someone.
	

	“The clash between duty (to have to care) and want (she wants to escape, be careless, be free). I found that tension very human and powerful.”

	Playing Lali is Victoria Luengo, reuniting with Gurrea in this bigger production after “Suro.”

	“Since ‘Suro,’ Victoria has become a dear friend. She happens to be one of the best actress that I have ever seen. So, I always want to work with her. When it was time, I offered her the part.”

	At that point, Lali was still evolving. Luengo became part of that process, helping to build a character who exists caught between her restlessness and her responsibility.

	“There was a draft of the script, but it was early stages. From that moment onwards, Victoria and I opened a process of workshopping ideas, trips to the desert where we first encounter Lali in the film, we gave Lali a past and we bounced many ideas. All of that influenced the later drafts Francisco Kosterlitz and I wrote for the script.”

	With “Saints,” intimate family drama collides with thriller and heist movie. Within and between the competing genres is always care.



	

	



	“There is a heart to the film: it is Lali’s relationship towards caring for her estranged mom Gloria. That is the internal. Then, there is an external journey, which relates to Rosario and her group.”

	Rosario and her gang bring Lali into the world of theft, but their approach to stolen religious objects is surprising.

	“That brings the thieving, the thrill and the heist, but also a knowledge of delicacy, appreciation and care. There is a certain ode to the gesture, which can connect to both the stealing and the caring.”

	Soon, the distinction between Lali’s two worlds begins to collapse. “Little by little, Rosario becomes like an alternative mother” the director said, “and when her people get inside Gloria’s house, the layers converge.”

	For Gurrea, these different versions of family and paying attention aren’t necessarily in opposition.

	“I think they are related and they feed each other. The type of care that I wanted to explore in the film, we can only do it if we take the time to appreciate, if we take into account, if we feel a connection. Be it objects or people.”

	That idea also complicates the film’s relationship with religion. The gang steals sacred objects, but their movements around them can resemble ceremony not desecration.
	

	Researching religious-art theft, Gurrea came across Erik the Belgian, a notorious thief who targeted churches across Spain during the 20th century.

	“The way he described the robberies – procedural, coordinated, silent – felt almost ritualistic to me. He also talked about the buyers’ feelings towards the stolen objects when delivered to them and it seemed like worship.”

	An irresistible contradiction.

	“I found these ideas very ambiguous and powerful and I wanted to explore them cinematically. After all, iconoclasm and idolatry could be understood as two faces of the same coin.”

	Her encounter with sacred objects does not simply turn into a rejection of the Catholic world associated with her mother. Instead, it creates space for another kind of discovery.

	“And here, between those two faces, between those two poles, Lali opens herself to some wonderment. Beyond duty and guilt, both very Catholic things, Lali discovers that she wants to be next to her mom in the last stages of their relationship.”

	After the rural setting of “Suro,” “Saints” moves into the city. That shift was one of the few things the director planned from the beginning.

	“The only really premeditated thing was to find fiction in the district where I live, so this was going to be an urban film.”

	Its tone, however, tracks its elusive protagonist.

	“I wanted it to be playful, because it is Lali’s nature.”

	And underneath the family tensions, robberies and shifting allegiances, Gurrea kept returning to one idea.

	“As per the rest, I wanted to make a film full of mystery. Both cinematic mystery but also playing with the idea of religious mystery.”

schema.headline: ‘Suro’ Director Mikel Gurrea on ‘Saints,’ Directing ‘The Belovd’ Star Victoria Luengo,  Religious-Art Theft and Finding Mystery in Care

title: Sean Gunn Says He’s ‘Too Old’ and ‘Retired’ From Playing Rocket Raccoon in ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’: It ‘Hurts After a While’
description: Sean Gunn has proclaimed himself “retired” from doing the on-set motion capture for the fan-favorite “Guardians of the Galaxy” character Rocket Racc
body:
Sean Gunn has proclaimed himself “retired” from doing the on-set motion capture for the fan-favorite “Guardians of the Galaxy” character Rocket Raccoon. The actor explained that he feels he’s aged out of standing in for the Marvel character due to the physical demands of contorting himself into the shape of the small animal on a recent episode of The Brandon Davis Show.

	“Since I’ve turned 50 a couple of years ago, I am retired from playing Rocket,” he said. “Not that they’ve called. But if they did, I don’t think that I could do the motion reference anymore for Rocket. I think I’m too old.”
	

	He continued: “Everyone thinks it’s my knees, but it’s really my feet and my ankles. I’m in a catcher’s crouch, and I’m pivoting a lot on my points of contact with the ground. I’m doing a lot of pivoting in my ankles and feet. And over the years, I think it had a little bit of an effect on my physiology.” He also noted that it “hurts after a while.”


	While Bradley Cooper famously voiced the character, it was Gunn who performed the aforementioned on-set motion capture for the animated raccoon. Gunn did this for the character in all three of the “Guardians of the Galaxy” movies, the first of which premiered in 2014. The sequel, “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2,” followed in 2017 and “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3” premiered in 2023.

	On-screen, Gunn also played the Marvel character Kraglin Obfonteri in “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2,” “Avengers: Endgame,” “Thor: Love and Thunder,” “The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special” and “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3.”

schema.headline: Sean Gunn Says He’s ‘Too Old’ and ‘Retired’ From Playing Rocket Raccoon in ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’: It ‘Hurts After a While’

title: ‘The Eternaut’ Star Ricardo Darín on Argentina’s Resilience: ‘We’re Like Peter Sellers in ‘The Party,’ the Bugler Who Never Dies’
description: The premise of Argentina’s Ricardo Darin’s latest feature, “Therapy Done Right” (Lo dejamos acá”), world premiering at the San Sebastian Festival, i
body:
The premise of Argentina’s Ricardo Darin’s latest feature, “Therapy Done Right” (Lo dejamos acá”), world premiering at the San Sebastian Festival, is deceptively simple: A pragmatic psychoanalyst loses faith in conventional methods and starts pushing the boundaries with his patients. Everything seems to be going well until a writer (played by Diego Peretti), struggling with creative block, walks into his office.

	The dark comedy, which Darin’s Kenya Films produced, is having a special screening at the fest before it streams worldwide Oct. 16 on Netflix. He tapped Hernán Goldfrid, who directed him on “Thesis on a Homicide,” to helm the feature.
	

	Darin and Goldfrid spoke to Variety at the tony Maria Cristina Hotel in San Sebastián:


	Ricardo, you play the psychoanalyst who rejects an award at the onset, stating that Argentina has the largest number of psychoanalysts in the world and yet the percentage of Argentineans with some form of mental health issue has doubled. Is this a fact?

	Yes, and I think it has something to do with the mix of cultures that shaped Argentina – Italians, Spaniards, Jews, Arabs, Germans… – really, a bit of everything. And I think that’s part of where it comes from. Argentina also embraced psychoanalysis a long time ago, and it’s worked for us. In many ways, it’s worked really well.

	Everyone has mental health issues. A lot of people around the world do – they just don’t realize it. They think there’s something else causing it. I think it’s worth clarifying that, because otherwise it might give the impression that Argentinians are the only ones with mental health problems. That’s not the case.
	

	But I also know there are more psychoanalysts in Argentina. There are a lot of psychoanalysts compared to other countries. Why is that? Nobody really knows. Because people have been drawn to studying it at university. Argentina has some very good universities for psychology and sociology.

	Hernán Goldfrid: I think it has a lot to do with what Ricardo was just saying. I really like the idea of laughing at ourselves while also taking a moment to reflect. I think that’s part of why Argentina, and Buenos Aires in particular, has such a high number of psychoanalysts. We have this tendency to dwell on our own neuroses, to reflect, to listen to our own inner voice – to really look at what’s going on inside us. The film taps into that and I think that’s exactly why it made us laugh. Because at the end of the day, it felt very human.

	Darín: We like to laugh at ourselves – it’s good for us. It’s a kind of balm. Yes, it’s healthy. And what about psychoanalysis? That doesn’t necessarily make us laugh, but the first step is to put into words what we think is happening to us and then compare that with what’s actually happening. And those two things can be very different.

	How did this project come to you and your company, Ricardo?

	“We received an early version of the story – a rough outline, a treatment-from our screenwriter, Emmanuel Díez, and it immediately caught our attention. At times, it made us laugh. It also gave us a chance to laugh at ourselves a little and reflect. So, we immediately brought Hernán on board to hear what he thought and see if he liked the idea. He did and he joined the writing process, as he likes to call it, and the three of us started having fun with the idea and shaping it together. But ultimately, he was the one who really gave it its final form, because he’s the director.

	What were you hoping to achieve with this film?

	Hernán Goldfrid: I think what we were really looking for was disruption. We talked about it at one point – the idea of being disruptive, unpredictable. We wanted the story to constantly put you up against the unexpected.

	Darín: And we take that to the extreme, because that’s what my character does – he takes everything to the extreme. And at that point, it becomes crazy, completely outrageous. He even goes into people’s homes.
	

	Goldfrid: It comes from this need our character has, a very pragmatic need to do something. Our character says, “You have to get your hands dirty.” And that’s really what drives him: getting directly involved in each of his patients’ emotional struggles, taking a completely hands-on approach.

	You had previously worked together on “Thesis on a Homicide” so did you develop a kind a shorthand to collaborate on this film?

	Darín: Yes, we already knew each other and we got along really well even back then. We had a great time. Hernán is very open and receptive. He really knows how to listen. He creates this back-and-forth dialogue, and that’s very encouraging for actors because he’s open to your ideas and gives you room to bring your own ideas into the process.

	And what were some of the challenges you faced during the shoot?

	Goldfrid: Every day on a film set is a challenge. Every situation is a challenge, because you’re suddenly confronted with everything you’ve been imagining and working toward for so long and now you have to make it real. There were definitely moments when we had to say, “Okay, now we’re standing on the edge of a cliff. What do we do?”

	But more than anything, we enjoyed it. I always say that filmmaking is a collective effort. It’s a team effort, and everyone brings their own knowledge and experience to the table. So throughout the process, we tried to make the most of what each person had to offer, so we could overcome those difficulties and challenges together – and, above all, enjoy the experience.

	We shot the film last year, and filming in Buenos Aires was also about making the city feel like another character in the story. The city runs through the film, and through the characters, and that was very important to us.

	And I imagine you also spoke with psychoanalysts and other professionals while developing the project?

	Darín: Yes, especially our screenwriter, Emmanuel. He spoke with several of them, and I think he still does.

	Goldfrid: You do a lot of research but the film is really about people. So the research was also about that – about human vulnerability. In that sense, it became much more personal. It was about getting into the emotional world of each of us. We did have some great conversations with professionals, but what we really wanted to explore was people. So part of the research was simply observing what happens to each of us when we’re faced with situations like the ones in the film.
	

	Darín: Hernán and I talked a lot. We laughed a lot, too. At first, we spent a lot of time laughing about the character, his extreme situations and the way he thinks. And little by little, the character started to take shape. Hernán was the one who kept everything in check and decided where to push it further and where to hold back, because it’s very easy to go too far.

	What’s next for you, Ricardo?

	Darin: I’m doing a play right now. It’s Bergman’s ‘Scenes from a Marriage,’ based on his famous film. I’m wrapping up the run in Madrid this coming Sunday, then I’m heading back to Argentina to take it on a short theater tour. And then next year I’ll be working on Season 2 of ‘The Eternaut‘ for most of the year. It’s going to be complicated, I don’t know if it’ll be even crazier, but it probably will be. No snow this time, but definitely crazier.

	And how do you feel about the current situation in Argentina with all the cuts to subsidies in the audiovisual sector?

	Darin: I think we’re at a bit of a turning point, a kind of pause, where we have to see how things settle. With an election year coming up, I imagine the Milei administration will highlight what it sees as its successes, while the opposition will emphasize what it sees as the government’s shortcomings. And we’re somewhere in the middle, trying to figure out what’s true and what isn’t.

	These days, it’s hard to know what’s true just by following the news—to tell the difference between the truth and a manipulated version of it. And that doesn’t just happen in Argentina; it happens all over the world.

	There have been a lot of cuts, not just to culture, but also in other very sensitive areas, such as disability services. There’s also a lot of discussion around a bill concerning disability rights and services currently being debated in Congress.

	Argentina is a country that’s used to crises. We’ve had a lot of practice surviving crises. So, nothing really scares us anymore. Somehow, we always survive and manage to move forward. Like in that movie ‘The Party’ with Peter Sellers. He’s playing the bugle and people are shooting at him, but he just never dies. Well, that’s us. We’re Peter Sellers.

schema.headline: ‘The Eternaut’ Star Ricardo Darín on Argentina’s Resilience: ‘We’re Like Peter Sellers in ‘The Party,’ the Bugler Who Never Dies’

title: Issa Rae Is ‘Never Going to Stop’ Using Her Power for Good, Even as Mergers and AI Disrupt Hollywood: ‘This Is All Men’s Fault’
description: Issa Rae received the Entertainment Entrepreneur of the Year Award at Variety’s L.A. Power of Women event on Wednesday in Beverly Hills. The award w
body:
Issa Rae received the Entertainment Entrepreneur of the Year Award at Variety’s L.A. Power of Women event on Wednesday in Beverly Hills. The award was presented by U.S. Bank senior executive vice president Courtney Kelso and honored the Emmy-nominated actress, writer, producer and entrepreneur.

	Rae created, executive produced and starred in HBO’s “Insecure,” which ended its run in 2021. Kelso welcomed Rae to the stage, saying the comedian has “put her own community here in L.A. front and center across her incredible ventures.”
	

	Rae began her acceptance speech by joking that she hadn’t written anything inspirational, as she’d been distracted by everything happening across the nation, “the industry [eating] itself,” climate disasters, politics and the rise of AI. But she did identify one force that continues to create instability: “This is all men’s fault. Rich, white men to be specific” she joked, drawing laughter from the audience.

	“It is hard to feel like a powerful woman when men keep fucking everything up,” she said.

	She then took a serious tone when detailing the struggles she’s faced, sharing that “it’s hard to feel inspired when you feel helpless and useless.”

	As a writer, Rae said she experiences those feelings often, but she has also learned that she can direct her energy toward the things she knows she can control.

	“I can decide who I’m around, who I work with, who I champion, who I invest in, whose stories I tell, who I platform, who I respond to,” she said. “I can use the power I do have to pour into my little community to make sure whatever success I’m lucky enough to have doesn’t stop with me.”
	

	She shared that “even when I’m tired, pissed off or deeply uninspired by what’s happening around me, I can honestly say that nothing can stop me from trying to figure out where I can be useful. Because as discouraged as I may get, I’m never going to stop trying.”

	Rae concluded her speech by saying, “Maybe that’s all any of us can do — is just figure out where we have some power and use it the fuck for good, please. So that’s what I’m going to do. I hope you guys do too.”

	Rae’s on-screen credits include Greta Gerwig’s “Barbie,” Cord Jefferson’s “American Fiction,” the “Black Mirror” episode “Hotel Reverie” and “A Black Lady Sketch Show,” which she also executive produced. She also voices Jessica Drew in Sony Pictures’ “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse” and Angela in the HBO Max series “Young Love.” As a producer, Rae worked on the 2023 film “Gray Matter” and executive produced the HBO Max series “Rap Sh!t.” She also produced “One of Them Days,” starring Keke Palmer and SZA. She is set to write and executive produce a new HBO comedy pilot, which is an untitled “male friendship show.”

schema.headline: Issa Rae Is ‘Never Going to Stop’ Using Her Power for Good, Even as Mergers and AI Disrupt Hollywood: ‘This Is All Men’s Fault’

title: Netflix’s ‘A Different World’ Is a Bold, Fun and Timely Reboot Centering the Uniqueness of Gen Z: TV Review
description: Thirty-nine years after the beloved NBC series premiered, Netflix is reopening the gates of the fictional, historically Black Hillman College with “
body:
Thirty-nine years after the beloved NBC series premiered, Netflix is reopening the gates of the fictional, historically Black Hillman College with “A Different World.” Created by Felicia Pride and executive produced by Debbie Allen (who helmed the first version of the sitcom), the bold and brilliant reboot follows Deborah Wayne (an outstanding Maleah Joi Moon), the vibrant youngest child of Whitley Gilbert-Wayne (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne Wayne (Kadeem Hardison). Artistic but flighty, Deborah ends up at her parents’ alma mater when an unfortunate incident gets her NYU Tisch School of the Arts acceptance rescinded. Timely and fresh, the new series distinguishes itself from the original while paying homage to everything that made its predecessor so iconic.
	

	The 10-episode first season, which chronicles an entire school year, opens amid the chaos of move-in day. Deborah is attempting to make sense of her schedule, but she isn’t the only one trying to find her footing at Hillman. She rooms with Rashida Duvall (Alijah Kai Haggins), a no-nonsense scholarship student from Compton who quickly grows frustrated with Deborah’s nepo-baby, scatterbrained antics. Rounding out their trio is Hazel (Kennedi Reece), a sweet, naive young woman, completely sheltered by her conservative upbringing but determined to follow her Michelle Obama dreams. In the boys’ dorm, Shaquile Johnson (Cornell Young IV), Deborah’s old flame and Ron Johnson’s (Darryl M. Bell) only child, hopes to put the Hillman football program on the map. Turning down a Division 1 university for Hillman, he finds himself rooming with Kojo (Chibuikem Uche), a Nigerian-Ghanaian U.K. transplant and Amir (Jordan Aaron Hall), a queer Harlemite piecing his life back together after a misstep or two.
	

	For a show about Gen Z characters — and certainly as a reboot or continuation — “A Different World” knocks it out of the park. The single-camera dramedy captures the unique experience of attending an HBCU in the 21st century while addressing issues like the current federal government’s retaliatory agenda against Black Americans, alongside expected themes like love triangles and financial aid woes in college. However, the series moves so fast that even the most focused viewer is likely to get whiplash.

	Amid varied stories and characters — new and old — it’s apparent that Pride and Allen have a distinct vision for this series. However, without the expansive 20-plus-episode seasons that were standard when the first series aired, storylines that would typically unfold over several episodes, or a season, are crammed into just 10 30-minute episodes. In Episode 7, “Sometimes You Get the Culture… Sometimes The Culture Gets You,” a thread about sexual health and wellness runs alongside a storyline involving Kojo about the diaspora wars and the end-of-year talent show performances. The episode is tightly written and woven together seamlessly. Yet the speed of “A Different World” leaves little time to breathe, or for the audience to settle in.

	Still, this rushed pace doesn’t take away “A Different World”’s dynamism. The series connects the generations seamlessly, letting cherished characters from the original show float in and out of the new one while giving the new faces the platform they deserve. The show works perfectly well as a standalone, but knowing the lore and history behind “The Cosby Show” spinoff and even Whitley and Dwayne’s romance will undoubtedly allow those viewers a well-layered experience.

	In addition to seeing the students and faculty grapple with the near non-existent federal funding due to the Trump administration, “A Different World” also infuses social media, a soundtrack that includes Summer Walker, Mariah the Scientist and Alex Isley, as well as several appearances by known artists (which was a staple of the original show). Moreover, it spotlights more than romantic relationships. Friendship breakups and breakdowns are a major theme, and audiences also get real insight into what Dwayne and Whitley’s lives have looked like for the last four decades.
	

	Netflix’s “A Different World” has a lot to live up to. The first series was a major cultural touchstone centering Black Gen Xers in a way never done before on television. The show was so monumental that HBCU enrollment rose by 26%, most likely due to the show’s popularity. By spotlighting the passions and ills they’ve inherited, the new iteration lets Gen Z share what matters to them as they address the particularities of the Black American experience. Fun, messy and absolutely enthralling, “A Different World” proves original IP can be honored while introducing something refreshingly new.

	“A Different World” is now streaming on Netflix.

schema.headline: Netflix’s ‘A Different World’ Is a Bold, Fun and Timely Reboot Centering the Uniqueness of Gen Z: TV Review

title: Isabel Sandoval, Tricia Tuttle, ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Producer Anup Poudel Join QueerFrames Mentor Lineup as Lab Unveils New Cohort, Southeast Asia Expansion (EXCLUSIVE)
description: QueerFrames Screenwriting Lab, a training initiative for emerging queer, trans and nonbinary filmmakers, is expanding into Southeast Asia for its fo
body:
QueerFrames Screenwriting Lab, a training initiative for emerging queer, trans and nonbinary filmmakers, is expanding into Southeast Asia for its fourth annual edition, bringing together storytellers from India, the Philippines, Vietnam, Singapore, Indonesia and the diaspora.

	The 2026 cohort features eight fiction feature projects, with queerness woven into the core of each story. The selected filmmakers are Alec Berame and Joshua Caesar Medroso from the Philippines, Saurav Mahind and Sanju Kadu from India, Minh-Anh Vo Dinh from Vietnam and Canada, Megan Teo from Singapore, Kurnia Alexander from Indonesia and Rachel Leyco from the U.S. Their scripts take on identity, intimacy, masculinity, belonging and personal freedom through love stories, thrillers, horror and dramedies that blend genres.
	

	Launched in 2023, QueerFrames has worked with 22 queer and trans filmmakers from the region since its founding. The Lab pairs craft-focused screenwriting development with mentorship from filmmakers, producers, programmers and industry leaders, taking participants from an early draft to a project that is ready for the market.


	The 2026 edition will open with an in-person screenwriting retreat in Hua Hin, Thailand, running Sept. 23 to Oct. 2, followed by an Industry Day in Bangkok on Oct. 3 held in partnership with the French Embassy in Thailand, Alliance Française Bangkok and the French Regional Audiovisual Cooperation. The Lab will then continue with virtual sessions through March 2027.

	Netflix and the French Institute in India are backing the 2026 edition, with additional support from Purin Film Fund in Thailand and Momo Film Co in Singapore.
	

	This year’s mentors include Anup Poudel, who produced Nepal’s Oscar contender “Elephants in the Fog,” winner of the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize at Cannes; Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle, returning to the Lab; Filipino filmmaker and actor Isabel Sandoval; “A Useful Ghost” director Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke; Indian screenwriter Gazal Dhaliwal; and Momo Film Co chief Tan Si En. Writer-directors Vishnu Sinha, adjunct faculty at Columbia University, and Paromita Dhar return as Lab instructors.

	“With this year’s expansion into Southeast Asia, QueerFrames is bringing together a wider community of storytellers who are pushing beyond familiar narratives and exploring queer lives across cultures, genres and lived experiences,” said Rafiul Alom Rahman, director of QueerFrames Screenwriting Lab. “Our hope is to build not just stronger projects, but lasting connections and infrastructure that enable these filmmakers to thrive.”

	“Some of the most powerful stories come from places and experiences that have been left out of the frame,” said Poudel. “QueerFrames offers writers the space to develop those stories with courage, specificity and creative freedom.”

	Mathieu Béjot, cultural attaché for film, audiovisual and digital content at the French Institute in India, pointed to the partnership’s longevity. “Our longstanding partnership with QueerFrames reflects that commitment, and we are delighted to continue supporting a new generation of queer filmmakers from South and Southeast Asia as they develop their work and connect with the wider international film ecosystem,” Béjot said.

	Among the 2026 projects: Berame’s “Hisap Sebatang Before Ciao! (Each/Other)” follows a Filipino diplomat navigating a geopolitical crisis while hiding a quiet romance with his counterpart from Malaysia. Vo Dinh’s “Anglerfish” centers on two men whose seaside getaway is upended by a stranger’s arrival and a string of grisly deaths. Teo’s “Pack” follows a closeted professional boxer who turns to underground pit-fighting to transition. Leyco’s “Winning” is a spoken-word dramedy about a broke queer artist who wins the lottery and slowly becomes the gambling-addicted father she despises.

	Mahind’s “Starvation” follows Namya, a gay drifter who pickpockets closeted men until one of his marks comes back looking for closeness instead of revenge. Kadu’s “Under Such a Sky” follows a closeted gay man who breaks his pattern of chasing straight men through a bond with four kids from his swimming class. Medroso’s “Lasto (Last Two)” follows a debt-ridden gay uncle and his niece tracking down the thief who robbed them of their winnings from a “lasto” game. Alexander’s “Jatuh Cinta yang Lurus (A Straight Way to Love)” follows a gay filmmaker who returns to the town that once cast him out, only to find that reconnecting with the friend who was also his first love threatens the life he rebuilt after leaving.

schema.headline: Isabel Sandoval, Tricia Tuttle, ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Producer Anup Poudel Join QueerFrames Mentor Lineup as Lab Unveils New Cohort, Southeast Asia Expansion (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘200 Lives, Paco Rabal,’ Told in the Spanish Screen Legend’s Own Voice, Boarded by Latido Films
description: SAN SEBASTIAN, Spain – Paco Rabal worked with Luis Buñuel, Michelangelo Antonioni and Carlos Saura, made more than 200 films and built a career span
body:
SAN SEBASTIAN, Spain – Paco Rabal worked with Luis Buñuel, Michelangelo Antonioni and Carlos Saura, made more than 200 films and built a career spanning Spain, France, Italy and Mexico. In “200 Lives, Paco Rabal,” the Spanish screen legend gets one more role: Narrator of his own life.

	Directed by Vanesa Benítez, the documentary world premieres as the closing film of San Sebastián Festival’s Made in Spain section. Latido Films handles international sales on the Spain-France-Mexico co-production, produced by Spain’s MLK Producciones and Horizon Media with France’s Plan B et Compagnie and Mexico’s Monstro Films.
	

	Its key discovery is a collection of cassette recordings Rabal recorded his memoirs on. Combined with his Super 8 films, photographs, videotapes and other family material, they allow the actor, who died in 2001, to drive the film himself.


	“Paco Rabal was and remains one of Spain’s and Europe’s top leading actors,” says Latido Films managing director Antonio Saura. “His versatility gave him innumerable recognitions, including a Cannes best actor award.”

	But it is the personal material, Saura argues, that provides the sales proposition with another dimension.

	“Here we find his life was as exciting as his talent, and listening to him narrate it, thanks to the amazing discovery of some self-recorded tapes, brings us a new perspective of his art and his life.”

	For Benítez, the challenge was to peer behind Francisco Rabal, the internationally celebrated actor, and find Paco, the boy from rural Murcia.

	“I think Paco was always himself, whether he was in front of a camera playing a role under the most famous director of the time or talking about his personal experiences in front of a tape recorder,” she told Variety.
	



	

	



	“When you listen to the cassettes on which he recorded his memoirs, you can picture him sitting at a bar, surrounded by his fellow townspeople.”

	Benítez avoids a conventional talking head biography. Other testimonies remain in voiceover, while Rabal’s recordings and archive drive a film structured partly as a last dream, with the actor looking back on his life at the moment of death.

	Hours spent watching his home movies, reading his diaries and listening to the tapes revealed dreams as a returning fascination.

	“He dreams of his loved ones who are no longer with him, of things that later happened to him in real life. He even found himself on trial in his dreams,” she said. “I believe that in dreams, despite being surrounded by so much fantasy, there is a great deal of truth.”

	They also show someone looking backwards.

	“Deep down, the one speaking was a child who wanted to return to the paradise of childhood,” Benítez explained.

	Rabal repeatedly returned to Cuesta de Gos in Murcia, where he had grown up, filming family scenes on Super 8. He died in Bordeaux while returning to Spain, having recently played Francisco Goya in Carlos Saura’s “Goya in Bordeaux,” a film which won him the Goya for best actor.

	“That is why, through cinema and, in a sense, a final dream, this film brings Paco back home,” Benítez said.

	Yet the doc-feature also uses him as a route through European and Latin American cinema.

	“Rabal’s journey offers the chance to look into all the film revolutions: from Mexico New Cinema to French Nouvelle Vague or Spain’s ’80s,” said producer José Antonio Hergueta.

	That international history even feeds the project’s co-production structure.

	“Fortunately Rabal is still remembered in France and Mexico, at least amongst mature generations and filmgoers,” Hergueta said. “We’ve focused on partners that would appreciate a quality documentary that, thanks to cinema, travels through the 20th century.”

	France was particularly attractive, he added, because of its established broadcast space for documentaries about cinema, actors and filmmakers.

	Rabal’s career had many politically divided lives. A star of Franco-era Spanish cinema, he would become associated with filmmakers and political currents distant from that world.
	

	“Paco was a person full of contradictions, and that’s also reflected in the documentary: his desires, his fears, his thoughts — so diverse and contradictory,” she said.

	What remained constant, Benítez argues, was his understanding of acting as work. “He never forgot his humble, working-class family background, despite all the egos, glitz and pretensions that are always swirling around the world of cinema.”

	Much of the material that makes that private side visible survived thanks to his wife, actor Asunción Balaguer, who spent decades preserving and organizing his archive.

	“It’s really the History of Cinema of the 20th Century — yes, with a capital ‘H’ and ‘C’ — as seen through his work,” Benítez said. “The value of all this is incalculable.”

	For Hergueta, the film also illustrates a broader challenge facing Spanish documentary: international co-production has advanced faster than the ability of many culturally specific films to reach audiences abroad.

	Spain has no shortage of “subject matters, stories and characters,” he argues. The work begins much earlier, in developing projects with international potential “from the very conception of the idea.”

	With Rabal, at least, that international dimension comes ready made with its subject.

schema.headline: ‘200 Lives, Paco Rabal,’ Told in the Spanish Screen Legend’s Own Voice, Boarded by Latido Films

title: ‘No One Achieves Anything Alone’: Inside Variety’s Power of Women Event With Jennifer Hudson, Sharon Stone, Pearlena Igbokwe and Melissa McCarthy
description: Jennifer Hudson, Pearlena Igbokwe, Melissa McCarthy and Sharon Stone were the guests of honor at the starry Variety Power of Women presented by Life
body:
Jennifer Hudson, Pearlena Igbokwe, Melissa McCarthy and Sharon Stone were the guests of honor at the starry Variety Power of Women presented by Lifetime event in Beverly Hills Wednesday night, during which the musician, executive and actresses were commended for both their outstanding accomplishments and their dedicated commitment to a number of key causes.

	The annual event, hosted by multi-hyphenate comedian Iliza Shlesinger, brought a long list of influential talents to a packed Beverly Hills Hotel for an evening centered on both the Power of Women honorees and the accomplished women profiled in the annual Women’s Impact Report, which highlights leaders in the entertainment industry. And while Hudson, Igbokwe, McCarthy and Stone all have much to brag about, each of the women used their time on stage to turn the focus to the charities they were supporting and highlight the many different ways the term “powerful” can be applied.
	

	Following introductory remarks from Variety‘s co-president and publisher Dea Lawrence, co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh and co-editor-in-chief Cynthia Littleton — plus a show-stopping opening performance of “I Will Always Love You” by Hudson — the first honoree of the night was Igbokwe, introduced by Queen Latifah. The chairman of NBCUniversal’s Television Studios, NBC Entertainment & Peacock Scripted, Igbokwe spent more than 35 years helping shape the medium of television across prestige cable, broadcast, studios and now streaming. She used her speech to support the nonprofit A Better Chance.
	

	“A Better Chance not only introduced me to Kent Place but also supported me when I got there with test-taking workshops, mentoring, and sometimes emotional encouragement — resources I would not have had otherwise. This set me up for an Ivy League education, transforming the trajectory of my life and that of my entire family,” she said. “So yes, my origin story started with hard work, but someone had to give me an opportunity. No one achieves anything alone.”

	After an introduction by Molly Sims, Paige DeSorbo took to the podium next to receive the Courage Award presented by the Purina Purple Leash Project, a charity that helps create pet-friendly shelters for survivors of domestic abuse. DeSorbo discussed opening up about her experience surviving an abusive relationship as a teenager, why she decided to speak about it on her podcast “Giggly Squad and how her cat, Daphne, helps her feel safe.

	“Daphne has been there for the version of me that nobody else sees,” she said. “She just curls up on my chest and purrs and everything, for a second, feels right again. No context needed. No story to tell. Just presence. I think that’s the incredible thing about our pets. They don’t need us to explain what we’re going through. They just stay. They give us a sense of safety and remind us that we are loved, even when we don’t feel our strongest. And that’s why the Purple Leash Project means so much to me.”

	“The Jennifer Hudson Show” was honored with the Variety Changemaker Award, presented by Waymo. Hudson, along with many of the show’s producers, accepted the award after an introduction by the company’s chief marketing officer, Suzanne Philion. Later in the evening, Hudson also took to the stage to spotlight the Jennifer Hudson Foundation and her show once more.

	“Our mission was always to highlight and accentuate the positive, and that is what we strive to do at ‘The Jennifer Hudson Show’ each and every day,” Hudson said. “That brings me to power. Power is an interesting idea. I think we’ve been taught to shy away from embracing power. We are told to be strong, never told to be powerful. But power can be good, and in the right hands, power can change the world for the better. And what better hands than those of a woman?” She continued: “Power can open doors, create a seat at the table, build a platform, protect a neighbor and lift a voice. So I am honored to be in a room where we’re celebrating power, good power.”
	

	Next, McCarthy’s former “Gilmore Girls” collaborator Lauren Graham welcomed her to the stage, and the “Bridesmaids” star used her time to shine the light on the Joyful Heart Foundation and two of the women in her life she considers powerful: Mariska Hargitay and Gloria Steinem. Steinem passed away earlier this month. “When I say powerful, I don’t mean tough or strong, though they certainly are. For me, the greatest display of power are those willing to roll up their sleeves and help bring change,” she said. “I am humbled to support the Joyful Heart Foundation, and I am honored to be a part of this room tonight. And I hope that we all can leave here inspired to roll up our sleeves and make a difference.”

	An acoustic rendition of “Motivation” by Normani helped lead in Emmy Award-nominated actress, writer, producer and entrepreneur Issa Rae, who received the Variety Entertainment Entrepreneur of the Year Award, presented by U.S. Bank senior executive vice president Courtney Kelso.

	“I can decide who I’m around for the most part, who I work with, who I champion, who I invest in, whose stories I help tell, who I platform, who I respond to,” said Rae. “I can use the power I do have to pour into my little community to make sure whatever success I’m lucky enough to have doesn’t stop with me. And even when I’m tired, pissed off, or deeply uninspired by what’s happening around me, I can honestly say that nothing can stop me from trying to figure out where I can be useful, because as discouraged as I may get, I’m never going to stop trying.”

	Sharon Stone closed out the night, taking the stage following remarks from actor and podcaster Marc Maron. The Academy Award-nominated, Emmy and Golden Globe-winning actress and producer reflected on her career and how she’s become the on- and off-screen icon she is today.

	“You have to claw your way to the top. So, for those of us who got here, it’s the top of our heads that broke that glass ceiling that you’re all getting the benefits of,” she said. “And I have gone the distance. I have gone the distance from being a sex symbol … and I did it by keeping both of these tired feet that hurt from wearing four-inch heels on poured concrete floors. I kept them firmly planted on terra firma because there is no gray in the red, white and blue. So the power that I feel in the power of women, I get because I am standing in the middle of you, and I do not stand alone when I stand here.”

title: Asia Video Content Spend to Hit $15 Billion in 2026 as Streaming and Local Film Draw Capital, Media Partners Asia Report Finds
description: Spending on video content in seven major markets across Asia is expected to climb to $15.1 billion in 2026, according to Media Partners Asia‘s “Asia
body:
Spending on video content in seven major markets across Asia is expected to climb to $15.1 billion in 2026, according to Media Partners Asia‘s “Asia Video Content Dynamics 2026” report. Streaming and local film account for nearly all new spending as television budgets shrink.

	The study covers India, Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. MPA puts 2025 spending across the seven markets at $14.8 billion and projects it will reach $15.4 billion by 2031.
	

	Television still takes about 60% of the total, against 30% for online video and 10% for film. Korea, at $6.9 billion, and India, at $5 billion, together made up roughly 80% of 2025 investment.


	“The viewership data shows demand is intact. Premium VOD engagement continues to grow across India, Korea and Southeast Asia, streaming now leads content investment in India, and local stories are winning at the box office from Hanoi to Jakarta and Mumbai. This is a story of reallocation rather than retreat as capital moves toward streaming and local film, where both audiences and returns are growing,” said Myat Pan Phyu, an analyst at MPA.

	The money picture is less rosy. The region’s media businesses have big audiences and plenty of creative talent, yet the report finds that this reach is not reliably turning into healthy profits. Many long-established companies trade well under their equity book value. In MPA’s view, the firms that build value will be the ones that spend capital wisely, trim costs and defend the content that genuinely sets them apart.

	India hit a turning point last year. Online video claimed 46% of the country’s content investment in 2025, edging past TV at 42% and taking the lead for the first time. Indian viewers logged 420 billion hours of online video over the year. JioHotstar holds a 58% share of premium VOD viewing in the country and has more than 180 million paying subscribers.
	

	In Korea, TVING ranks a clear second in the market behind Netflix. Indonesian platform Vidio, which leads its home market with more than 6 million paying subscribers, has been EBITDA-positive since the fourth quarter of 2025.

	Sports rights are what set streamers apart, according to MPA. Cricket helped push JioHotstar’s connected-TV reach up 26% during the 2026 Indian Premier League cricket tournament, while exclusive KBO baseball coverage took TVING from 5.3 million to 6.5 million subscribers. Coupang Play has built the widest premium sports offering in Korea. Vidio spreads Indonesian football, the Champions League and the Premier League across its pricing tiers. In Vietnam, the FIFA World Cup lifted premium VOD viewing by 22% this year.

	The report picks out local film as the clearest opportunity for growth in the region. In Vietnam, box office grew 20% to $213 million in 2025, with homegrown titles taking 69% of receipts. Indonesian box office rose 10.5% to $325 million, 60% of it from local films. India set a box office record of $1.41 billion. In Korea, a stronger domestic lineup is fueling a sizable theatrical rebound in 2026.

	Television looks weaker. People are still watching, but the revenue keeps slipping. Thai TV advertising dropped 18% to $422 million in 2025, and MPA says several markets are carrying more broadcast capacity than their ad income can support.

	Producers are feeling the squeeze too. Broadcasters and streamers have grown choosier about what they order, which hurts companies that live on production fees. Value is moving toward integrated studios and toward producers that own IP, have repeat buyers or earn money from several sources. Production in Korea costs more than anywhere else in Asia, and drama margins there have been compressed to between 5% and 10%. Southeast Asia is cheaper, but tighter commissioning is hitting it as well.

	“Asia’s video industries are not short of audiences or creative capability. They are short of structures that convert both into sustainable returns. As the margin for error narrows, management quality will become decisive. Companies that rationalize legacy costs through restructuring and the adoption of new technologies such as AI, collaborate where independent investment no longer makes sense and protect the content that gives viewers a reason to stay will increasingly outperform, and the valuation gap between winners and losers will widen,” said Stephen Laslocky, vice president at MPA.
	

	Of the seven markets, MPA sees India and Korea as furthest along the road to consolidation. India set the pace with a definitive transaction – the 2024 merger of Reliance’s Viacom18 and Disney’s Star India that created JioStar – and more M&A could follow. Korea is looking to the proposed TVING-Wavve combination to unlock value. Southeast Asia has lagged, though the firm sees clear scope for collaboration and consolidation in the Philippines, Thailand and Indonesia.

	Separately, MPA estimates that reorganizing CJ ENM into four clearly defined businesses could support an equity valuation far above the company’s current market value.

title: San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference: 10 Takeaways From AI to ‘Obsession,’ YouTube and Why International Movies Could Dominate the Oscars
description: It wasn’t just a sea breeze and late summer sun which brought a sense of new airs and targeted optimism blowing through the San Sebastian’s 2026 Cre
body:
It wasn’t just a sea breeze and late summer sun which brought a sense of new airs and targeted optimism blowing through the San Sebastian’s 2026 Creative Investors’ Conference.

	For four years, CIC, co-organized with CAA Media Finance, has insisted on upsides and opportunities in drastic post-COVID and post-peak TV downturn.

	2026 presented one clear example, in record summer U.S. box office — so panelists talking up dramatic U.S theatrical rebound. Other interviewees spoke large about new sources of energy galvanizing — and complicating —  the sector: the build of select national industries around the world, and an ever growing involvement of equity investment in financing.
	

	That said, the market at large in TV sell belabors at 75% of peak TV levels, as Ampere Analysis points out. Huge problems in key markets, moreover, remain. One case in point: In Christine Vachon’s lapidary phrase, U.S. independent production is “basically fucked up.”

	The Rebound

	“I think it’s a recovery; it’s a phenomenal result,” said Neon head of distribution Elissa Federoff at a key first day CIC panel, The New U.S. Landscape. “Every year since the pandemic, we have seen growth, and it’s been amazing to watch. “COVID happened, strikes happened, theater closures happened, and in that time, there has been a rise of a lot of other channels of entertainment, gaming, social platforms, streaming platforms. We’ve seen opportunities for new pathways during this point,” added Federoff, a major cheerleader for optimism at the Conference.

	Social Media: Friend No Foe
	

	Those pathways run through the very phenomenon, the explosion of social media, which was once seen as detracting from cinema audiences. “People are coming back to the movie theaters but engaging with movies in different ways,” said Sumerian’s Pictures’ Rob Williams. Cinemagoers now mostly find their movies on social media, Federoff notes. It is creating fandom, new audiences, with most cinemagoers now “younger, Millennial, Gen Z and even younger,” she noted.

	Reaching Out to the New Gen Crowd

	Launched in June 2025, and moving waves with its pick up of “Josephine” at Sundance, Sumerian Pictures often targets an audience that parent company Sumerian Records has been able to build on the music side, which is a younger audience that obviously cares about music,” noted Williams. Playing to social media, distributors are looking for movies to create conversations around,” noted Adele Romanski at producer Pastel Pictures. This context does much to explain the excitement around films like queer epic “La Bola Negra,” winner of the often Oscar predictive TIFF People’s Choice Award, which has a pop sensibility, mainstream reach and embraces the LGBTQ cause.

	‘Obsession,’ ‘Backrooms’ Drive the Conference, Festival Conversation

	So much of the conversation at the Conference, even on the panel Europe’s Current Challenges and Opportunities, turned on U.S. box office sensations “Obsession,” based on a YouTube short, and “Backrooms,” which began life as a viral YouTube web series. “‘Obsession’ and ‘Backrooms’ are two movies that completely changed the way Hollywood is talking about films,” said the L.A.-based Lorenzo de Maio on the panel. “Distributors need to bring the movie to the audience, and Curry [Barker] and Kane [Parsons] brought their own audiences. That same phenomenon is also felt in Europe. “There is an audience that loves movies, a younger audience, too, and that is open to different authentic voices in a way five or 10 years ago we wouldn’t have been that confident about,” noted StudioCanal’s Ron Halpern. “That’s a great thing for all of our local or mixed-language productions.” On the Andrew Garfield-Florence Pugh two-hander “We Live in Time,” for example, Halpern’s team knew Pugh would “deliver the TikTok audience,” and she did.
	

	International Films Oscar Domination?

	“We are [now] seeing at least three-four international films in the best film category,” said Rodrigo Teixeira, behind “I’m Still Here.” “And in five years from now, I believe international films will make up 60% of the category for best film, because we can talk more. We have freedom of speech, and in the U.S., without freedom of speech, it’s difficult to get financed.” Certainly, Teixeira, who broke out producing U.S. independents — “Francis Ha,” “The Witch” —  is now, beyond movies from James Gary, such as “Paper Tiger,” is now shooting films all over the world: in 2025 two in Brazil and Romania, and one in the U.S., Chile, Argentina and Lebanon.

	International Still Hurts

	Another factor driving international: co-Production. “There are so many opportunities to co-pro within Europe and so many ways of doing it. The complexity is there, but it’s worth navigating it because it’s a thriving industry,” said De Maio. And yet, international is hurting in multiple key markets and a myriad of ways. In Brazil, “I’m Still Here” and “The Secret Agent” made “exceptional” box office, “The Blue Trail” had “very good solid results,” said Teixeira. “But a lot of other Brazilian films make 10,000 admissions in theaters. And that kills the film.” In South Korea, “companies are increasingly looking internationally,” noted Heejeon Kim at Barunson C&C. That is “out of necessity,” she added at the Producing and Financing Across Borders panel. “The number of films and the revenues, everything’s shrinking, financiers are really struggling to invest money,” she added.

	Equity Builds as Key Financing, and Not Just in the U.S.

	Another challenge and strength in international: “What we’ve seen in the last decade in many, many countries is that local films’ market share has grown: People want to see local films. Indonesia’s cinema market share is now 60%. 10 years ago, it was probably 10%, 12% or 15%. That’s a major challenge for us,” Goodfellas’ Vincent Maraval said in a key Conference observation. So sales agents and producers are turning to equity to make up a shortfall not only in pre-sales but streamer pull-back and falling broadcaster pre-buy moneys. Having U.S. equity come into the European market is “a new thing” for Why Not Productions, said Pauline Lamy. “Because we can not pre-sell a lot of films because of their language, having that type of money is really helping us make films at a bigger scale. ‘Fjord’ needed that; ‘Emilia Pérez’ needed that. A lot of films couldn’t work without this mixed system.”
	

	Spain SETTs New State Aid Agenda

	It’s not just films’ private sector which is getting into the act, however. The CIC kicked off, fittingly enough, with the presentation of SETT, a go-getting Spanish sovereign venture capital fund, and part of Spain’s Ministry of Digital Transformation. Financed by E.U. Next Generation funds, and an innovation in state aid mindset for Spain, SETT does not give subsidies nor project financing but rather invests up to 49% of the equity of companies requiring 51% private sector participation, said SETT audiovisual director María Coronado. SETT has plowed €216 million in 15 operations, across the whole audiovisual value chain, generating a total investment of €445 million, she added. At the Conference, execs from three beneficiaries — Casa Mundo Cero, Aurora Media and Itaca Films —  talked up the benefits.

	Pijama: Pablo and Juan de Dios Larraín’s Groundbreaking New TVOD Platform

	“80%, 85% of movies that go to major film festivals in the world do not get distribution, and there’s no way to see them,” Pablo Larrain said at the Conference. And even if films do score distribution, rights can quickly lapse. Incredible but true: By Cannes 2026, Justine Triet’s 2023 Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Anatomy of a Fall” could not be seen in parts of Africa and Australasia. Enter Pijama, talked up by the Larrain brothers at CIC, a TVOD system affording global or select territory access and right holder returns, which get 80% of revenues, to great films audiences can’t see. Uploading costs $100 for two years. So far Pijama has cut deals with MK2, Alpha Violet and Visit Films, among sales agents. In Pijama’s Top 10 Emir Kusturica’s “Black Cat, White Cat” ranks at No. 4, Juliette Binoche’s “In-I In Motion” No 5. Any producer can upload a film.

	AI: Tool and Taboo

	A Thinking Towards the Future closed the 2026 Creative Investors’ Conference. Inevitably, it talked a lot about AI.

	“I think there’s paranoia, like the old saying there’s nothing to fear but fear itself. AI is a tool. AI is not something that is coming in and making movies,” said Ryan Kavanaugh at Acme AI & FX, one of its best known practitioners. “AI makes the below-the-line cost of movie drop by two thirds,” reduced a shoot schedule on one movie, shot entirely on a gray stage, from 70 to 19 days, allowed it to use exotic locations. “One of the beautiful parts of AI is you can literally make part or all of a movie in a manner not fit for theatrical release, but enough so a studio can watch it and they can make a decision on green light, Kavanagh added. “When you do a movie, you have a limited budget, whatever the budget is,” said Patrick Wachsberger, at 193. “Can you make this movie bigger in scope using AI? I’m not suggesting at all that you use AI for any of the actors, but if you want to do extension or whatever, something to give scope to the movie, I’m all for it.”

            JTT was then arrested at the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff's Station's jail on Monday ... jail records show. He was released a short time later.
      
    
            We reached out to a rep for JTT who had no comment.
